description: I’m an eighth-grade student interested in aerospace engineering, robotics, and solving real-world problems. I’m designing a 3D-printed RC car using Onshape and enjoy learning how mechanical systems work. Through NASA Space Apps, I hope to develop new skills, collaborate with others, and turn creative ideas into useful solutions.
summary:
We built Sky Motion Atlas to help people explore a simple question: what changed between two images of space?

Our website lets users investigate Barnard’s Star, R Draconis, 3I/ATLAS, Earth, and Mars using real observation images. Users can blink between two dates, play through 24 frames, and try different wavelength bands where available. They first look for changes themselves, then click “Reveal change” to see highlighted features, image comparisons, and measurements.

For the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge, we wanted to make comparing observations easier for people without an astronomy background. We also explain why an image might look different: a shift could come from camera alignment, and a brighter spot could be affected by wavelength or image quality.

Our goal is to help students and curious visitors explore NASA data, record what they notice, and understand what evidence they would need before calling something a discovery.
details:
What it does

What Moved? Sky Motion Atlas is a public web tool that turns real NASA SPHEREx observations into an investigation anyone can run in a browser. A visitor picks a target (Barnard's Star, the variable star R Draconis, or the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS) and steps through 24 real SPHEREx exposures in each of the telescope's six infrared detector bands. They can blink two dates, play the frames like a little video, drag a divider across two images, or view them side by side. When they are ready, "Reveal change" outlines a matched feature and estimates its apparent shift. On Barnard's Star it shows about 6.4 arcseconds over 262 days, labeled as an image-pattern estimate, not a confirmed measurement. Visitors then write what they noticed and an alternative explanation in a notebook, and export a dated evidence card with both images, observation IDs, credits and limitations.

How it works

A Python build script queries NASA/IPAC's IRSA archive for SPHEREx exposures covering each target. For the comet, it uses IRSA's published table of predicted positions. It downloads small FITS cutouts through IRSA's cutout service and uses each exposure's world coordinate system (WCS) to place them on one shared north-up sky grid (192 × 192 pixels, 1.6 arcseconds per pixel). One brightness stretch is applied per band, so frames can be compared. The site holds 432 SPHEREx frames (3 targets × 6 bands × 24 frames). Every frame keeps its observation ID, UTC time and a link to its archive record (the "observation passport"). The prepared frames are bundled with the site, so the demo works instantly even when the archive is slow. Bonus pages apply the same comparison method to Earth (GOES-19 weather satellite) and Mars (Curiosity rover photos).

Benefits

No account, download or coding is needed. It works on a laptop or a phone, and every view has a shareable link. Every image is real data that can be traced back to NASA's archive. Students learn to compare evidence carefully instead of treating every difference in an image as a discovery.

Intended impact

SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months in 102 colors of infrared light, but its archive is built for researchers. Our goal is to make that archive approachable for students, teachers, astronomy clubs and curious visitors. A short guided mission takes about 90 seconds and ends with a notebook and an evidence card a teacher can check. The habit we want to build is the same one astronomers used to find Pluto: observe, compare, question, and keep the evidence.

Tools, languages and software

HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no framework) for the website; Python 3.12 with Astropy, NumPy and Pillow for downloading and processing the FITS images; Vercel for hosting; GitHub and GitHub Actions for version control and automated checks; Playwright for browser tests on desktop and phone layouts; Google Fonts (DM Sans, Space Grotesk). No special hardware was used.

AI use: the code was written with help from OpenAI Codex, and the demo slides and this project description were drafted with help from Claude. We reviewed and tested the results ourselves.

What makes it creative

It turns blinking, the same technique that found Pluto in 1930, into an interactive game: look for the change yourself first, then press "Reveal change" to see the answer with an honest label. Other features: the observation passport for every frame, a downloadable evidence card, a field guide to the six infrared bands with a short quiz, a "Present" mode for classrooms, and a path explorer for an interstellar comet.

Factors we considered

Scientific honesty: the app never claims a discovery or a measured motion. It states that the star's core is saturated, that wavelength varies across each detector, that quality flags are not masked yet, and that comet positions are predictions, not detections.

No invented frames: frames switch directly between real observations, with nothing generated in between. The star fields stay on a fixed sky grid so real motion stays visible.

Reliability: the data is bundled, so the demo works even when the archive is slow.

Accessibility: keyboard controls, labels for screen readers, a pause control, respect for reduced-motion settings, and a phone layout.

Privacy: notebook notes stay in the visitor's browser.

Next steps: live search by any sky coordinates (RA and Dec), the challenge's other test targets (Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855 and RW Aurigae), quality-flag masking, and aligning images on background stars so estimates can become measurements.
